title: Orcas Are Smashing Sunfish Like Piñatas
summary:
Imagine a piñata at a birthday party. Now imagine an orca. Scientists have filmed orcas doing something wild: slamming into sunfish hard enough to make them explode.

In 2024 and 2025, researchers watched this in the Gulf of California. One adult orca held a dead sharp-tail sunfish steady. A second orca rammed into it — smashing the fish to bits.

"I was absolutely gobsmacked," said Marianne Nyegaard, a marine biologist in New Zealand who wasn't part of the study. "I thought it was the coolest thing I had ever seen."

Why do they do it? Maybe to break the huge fish into smaller bites for young orcas. After one explosion, a young orca ate the small pieces. Sharp-tail sunfish can grow up to 10 feet long — that's taller than a basketball hoop!

Or maybe it's just fun. Orcas are super social and clever. They work as a team to hunt blue whales, knock penguins off ice, and more.

"Killer whales are highly social animals," said marine biologist Francesca Pancaldi. One activity can give them food, help them bond, and teach young orcas how to hunt.

The study came out July 23 in Frontiers in Ethology.
why_it_matters: Watching how orcas work as a team and teach their young shows kids how much animals learn from each other, and why the ocean's food chains are worth protecting.

background_read: Orcas (also called killer whales — they are actually the biggest members of the dolphin family) live in oceans all over the world and stay in family groups called pods.
The Gulf of California (a long, narrow sea between Mexico's mainland and the Baja California peninsula) is famous for its whales, dolphins, and sea turtles.
Sunfish (huge, round fish with flat bodies) are some of the heaviest bony fish in the sea, even though they look strange to many people.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers studying orcas, plus marine biologists Marianne Nyegaard (in New Zealand) and Francesca Pancaldi, who gave their reactions.
WHAT: Orcas were filmed holding a dead sharp-tail sunfish steady and ramming it so hard that the fish exploded, and a young orca ate the small pieces.
WHERE: The Gulf of California, in 2024 and 2025; the study came out July 23 in Frontiers in Ethology.
WHY: The behavior may give the orcas food, help them bond as a group, teach young orcas how to hunt — or it might just be fun.

perspectives.description: They call the footage the coolest thing they have ever seen, because it shows a surprising new orca hunting behavior that nobody had filmed before.
Sunfish are living animals being smashed to bits, which can look upsetting. But scientists point out this is natural hunting, not cruelty.
Orcas are clever, social top predators with no natural enemies. They say more observations are needed to know whether this is mostly hunting practice, play, or teaching.
